You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game—tokens kept privately give me 1 point but cost each other member 0.3, while tokens placed in the group account seem to pay only the contributor 0.3 points without affecting others, which seems like an unusual twist on the typical setup I need to verify carefully.

Doing the math: if everyone keeps all 20 tokens privately, each person nets 1 point per token to self minus 0.3*20*3 from the others' tokens, working out to 20 total; if everyone instead puts all 20 into the group account, each nets 6 instead, for 24 total—so full cooperation via the group account is actually Pareto-superior here despite individual incentives favoring private tokens.

This is a repeated 10-round game, so the first-round choice matters for signaling. Since defecting is only tempting by 0.7 points per token and cooperation benefits everyone, I'll start by putting all 20 tokens into the group account to try to establish a cooperative norm.

Checking marginal incentives, keeping an extra token nets +1 to yourself but costs 0.3 from reduced group returns, leaving a positive 0.7 gain, so keeping tokens is individually dominant even though full group contribution (everyone gets 42) beats full defection (everyone gets 20). Breaking it down: keeping a token nets me +0.7 personally compared to contributing it, but costs others 0.3 each. Individually, keeping everything is the dominant strategy, giving a Nash equilibrium where everyone keeps all 20 tokens—even though full contribution would actually be socially optimal since the group-level payoff from contributing (0.3) exceeds the net social gain from keeping (0.1).

Since this is a repeated 10-round game, though, pure selfishness in round 1 might not be the best call—cooperation could be sustained through conditional strategies if I signal willingness to contribute early. I'm weighing whether to keep everything to maximize my own points, or contribute something to test if others reciprocate, since mutual cooperation yields 24 each per round versus 20 from mutual defection. I'm leaning toward a partial contribution as an opening move to probe cooperation without risking everything.
